By February, six months after the July work was committed, the first integration test against origin/main failed silently. The 43 unmerged commits from the 10 worktrees—the real implementation of system_v5 and system_v7 refactoring—never made it to main. Instead, what landed was the v9 scaffolding commit: 6,637 lines of JSON configuration stubs defining class signatures, function names, import paths. The Python beneath it was hollow: 1,234 lines of `pass`, empty methods, stub return values. The July work—real business logic, database adapters, validation pipelines—lived in the worktrees at f0afdc36a and claimgate/bypass-regression. # Premortem: Codex-Ratchet Merge-Base Failure

## THE FAILURE STORY

On merge day, when the team attempted to consolidate the 43 unmerged commits across the 10 worktrees back into origin/main, git's three-way merge algorithm silently used the wrong ancestor. Each worktree had been created from claimgate/bypass-regression (6e362506a), but origin/main had advanced beyond that point (a9909489 is 6,637 lines of scaffolding commits ahead). The automatic merge-base detection should have found the true common ancestor, but instead it used 6e362506a as the baseline—the very point from which the worktrees had split.

On July 16, the system_v5 track decided to deprecate and delete `validators/base.py`, moving all validation logic into a new consolidated `validation_core.py`. Seven files had their imports rewritten. That same day, system_v7 was adding new constraint-checking methods to `base.py`—the same file—without knowing deprecation was underway. ## THE FAILURE STORY

The v5/v7 refactor was tightly coupled—v5 defined shared schemas and import paths, v7 consumed them. The 43 commits came from 10 worktrees running in parallel, each with a complete local picture but no global view of dependencies. When merging to main chronologically (July 15–18 order), a v7 consumer commit (July 16) landed before the v5 provider commit (July 18) it depended on. Python import resolution broke silently; the symbol simply didn't exist yet on main. Subsequent commits in the queue landed on top of broken code. By the time the actual v5 definition arrived four commits later, downstream code had already layered invalid assumptions on top—assignments to undefined names, circular imports where v7 now imported v5 which imported utilities that now imported v7.
